content:
I have been working on a project to find Turyn Type sequences.

TT(n) is a collection of four sequences of the numbers {-1, +1} : 3 of length n, 1 of length n-1, whose combined autocorrelations sum to 0 for every non-zero shift.

Turyn-type sequences can be used to generate Hadamard Matrices, and in particular, TT(56) can be used to generate an Hadamard matrix of order 668, which is the smallest one for which no construction is known.

The main work I've been doing has to do with generating and optimizing a custom SAT solver, but along the way I've formalized (or rather had Aristotle formalize) several papers from the literature around these sequences:

https://github.com/tangentstorm/turyn/tree/main/lean/Turyn

I can't say that these proofs are in great shape yet. (They run and validate but the code is quite ugly in places).

One small win has been the discovery (by Codex / GPT5.4) of a previously unknown property shared by every known Turyn-type sequence: the pairwise product of the first two sequences is an anti-palindrome.

(By itself, this fact would cut the search space by 2^(n/2 -1), though it seems in practice some of that has already been accounted for by other common search techniques).

Anyway, the conjecture by Codex turned out to be true, as I was able to get Claude + Aristotle to produce a formal proof of it in Lean:

https://github.com/tangentstorm/turyn/blob/main/lean/Turyn/XY.lean#L491

The other files are mostly there to help me understand the exact pipeline of converting TT(56) -> Hadamard(668). I intend to clean them up to the point that I can understand them (which right now, I don't.)

I think this is premature to announce, personally.

Unless there is a clear entry point, something along the lines of "this file only imports Mathlib, and contains an easy-to-audit definition of Hadamard matrices and Turyn sequences, and this other file contains the statement Theorem 37.42 from Paper A, and this other file contains the statement TT(56)->Hadamard(668), and none of these files import unread-by-me AI code, and finally file X.lean (which may import all sorts of AI generated code) validates under comparator and gives the proofs of these statements", then I'm not sure what the purpose of announcing "I have thrown an AI at this problem and have nothing interesting to show for it" is.

I'm not trying to be mean --- I really like using AI in Lean and I think the possibilities are amazing! --- but I want to try to steer people towards doing this "properly" to the extend I understand it.

Well, I was mostly just sharing my experience, but okay.

The interesting thing to me was that actual mathematicians have been writing automated searches for these sequences for 20+ years, and they always take weeks or months to run, and when I pointed an AI at their data, it noticed a pattern they'd missed, and then when I pointed some more AI at that pattern, I got back a formal proof that the pattern is real, and can actually make a dent in the search space.

If I hadn't gotten a proof back, I wouldn't have been able to make the optimization in the search program.

Anyway, I thought it was a cool story, and I have nobody else around to share it with, so I posted it here.

Should we create a sort of guide to using comparator sort of like https://leanprover-community.github.io/did_you_prove_it.html, but more directed at setting up Comparator / Trusted Definitions? I found https://github.com/frenzymath/Anderson-Conjecture to be a good example of how one should set this up.

@Michal Wallace (tangentstorm)

The problem is that we would have to expend quite a bit of time to check this cool story, with a considerate non-zero risk of it being wasted.

The best way forward in my opinion, is to provide a comparator proof against the Formal Conjectures Hadamard Matrix of Size 668 Statement. That would be a near zero effort, to check (assuming the Formal Conjectures Statement is correct).

This way we would know this is indeed a cool story and you would have certainty that the Agent didn't trick / lie / cheat. I would be interested in either outcome.

I would second the need for a Comparator guide. It would be great if the standard for all large AI projects, especially ones solving open problems, was to use Comparator to isolate and check the main theorem.

And even if the project doesn’t exactly fit the comparator framework (because formalizing the main theorem statement is nontrivial involving many files of new definitions), it would be still useful to have have standards on how to make Comparator-compatable challenge files which act as a form of unit tests. For example one could use comparator to check a nontrivial consequence of the theorem, or use comparator (although I’m not yet sure how) to check that their new definitions satisfy important properties (similar to what was done in the LTE).

@Franz Huschenbeth there is no such proof, because nobody has yet found a Hadamard matrix of order 668.

If I gave you an Hadamard matrix of order n, you could look at it and make sure there's nothing in it but -1 and 1 values, and then square it and you would get nI (where I is the identity matrix of that size).

That's the entire definition of Hadamard matrices. You don't need lean to check it.

The Hadamard Conjecture is that such a matrix exists for all n=4*k, and nobody knows how to prove that.

We do know how to prove it for various classes of numbers (all powers of two, a couple small ones Hadamard found by hand, p+1 for primes p ≡ 3 (mod 4) and 2(p+1) for primes p ≡ 1 (mod 4)... any product of any of those, etc.)

There is also a complicated procedure by which you can take something called a Turyn-type sequence, turn it into a "T sequence", then turn that into a "base sequence" and so on, and out comes the Hadamard matrix. I don't fully understand the steps, so I had the AI formalize that pipeline so I could study it. The resulting proof is kind of a mess, but less of a mess for me than trying to understand a pile of unformalized papers.

In 2000, a team put out a paper trying to catalog and categorize all the known Turyn-type sequences, and they came up with an equivalence relation to categorize them, and a canonical form to select a unique representative of each class. That's formalized in Equivalance.lean.

Searching only for the canonical form cuts the search space by 2^10 (the size of each class), but it's still a huge search space, because you're starting with 2^(4n-1)... And the n we care about is 56.

The new/interesting thing is that the first two sequences in TT(n), when pairwise multiplied, seemed to always form an anti-palindrome. If that's true, then you can potentially cut another 2^(n/2 -1) configurations out of the search.

The statement of that fact is at the bottom of XY.lean:

theorem xy_product_law {n : Nat} (S : TurynTypeSeq n) (hn : 4 ≤ n)
    (hc : Canonical1 n S) :
    ∀ k, 2 ≤ k → k ≤ n - 1 → uAt S (n + 1 - k) = -(uAt S k)

(Where U is the product I mentioned of the first two sequences.)

That seems like a pretty clear and readable statement to me, and lean believes it's true. If you want to verify it you could just open the files in lean and see if they build.

But... I thought this was a forum where people could talk about lean. I'm not publishing a paper here. I'm just talking in a forum about a piece of software I'm using, and how it provided some value to me. Is that not allowed?

Are you guys all basically Andrew Wiles, sitting in your attic for years working on things until they're done before you mention it to anybody?

If not, where's the right place to just talk about something you're working on?

Well to my understanding this is a channel, where you announce a interesting Project / Result that was achieved using AI (and Lean well cause this is a Lean Zulip). If you do so then you can expect your project / result to be put under scrutiny from a Lean Perspective.

The problem is that "it builds in Lean" is technically pretty worthless, if you dont trust the proofs /definitions. This is where comparator comes in, as it really makes sure that the proofs did not cheat, Lean is a general purpose programming language so there are some ways to cheat (See for example the section "Specification-Based Evaluation: A Higher Standard for Correctness" of https://www.math.inc/formalqualbench). Furthermore all the relevant new definitions (and closure e.g. TurynTypeSeq, Canonical1) of them, should be placed into the Challenge.lean, so they can be readily trusted.

The reason I mentioned the Hadamard(668) Statement from the Formal Conjectures Repo was that you could used it to verify the pipeline from TT(56) -> Hadamard(668), in which case you would have certainty that what you are reading / trying to understand is correct. But I do see, that it was a bit pushy, so sorry for that.

I think you could quite easily point a Agent at the repo and let it create a copy in which the relevant results are placed into a Results.lean file, while the rest is in a Proof Directory and have it verify the proofs with Comparator, but of course this is up to you.

The reason we are nitpicky here is, that as @Jason Rute also mentioned, it's important to have a higher standard on AI generated proofs / results. In this case it might not be enormously important, but it might become more important in the future, so it is good to spread the word.

Michal Wallace (tangentstorm) said:

https://github.com/tangentstorm/turyn/blob/main/lean/Results.lean

Nice, for context it helps to include the config too then 

{
    "challenge_module": "Results",
    "solution_module": "Proofs",
    "theorem_names": [
        "Turyn.Result.tt_implies_hadamard",
        "Turyn.Result.canonical_form_exists",
        "Turyn.Result.xy_interior_antipalindrome"
    ],
    "permitted_axioms": ["propext", "Quot.sound", "Classical.choice"],
    "enable_nanoda": false
}

Not a comparator expert, but it looks okay looking at Proofs and Results.

It does concern me a bit that it looks like it is largely or solely Claude setting up the comparator though, just intuitively seems like that part could do with a human touch, it could technically change a bunch of other things at the same time and maybe make it do some nonsense, though seems unlikely.

Another issue is that comparator just verified whether what you have proven is correct, but if you used any of your own definitions this may not be the same as what you thought you have proven in math terms.

I don't know how much this is an issue in this run, I can see you defined TurynTypeSeq , Canonical , Equivalent etc . yourself for instance, but something to keep in mind, along the lines of what Kim was saying.

Edit: Looking more into it, it appears a huge amount is your own / AI definitions, so with that in mind comparator is limited in what it tells you, without a lot of human verification of definitions too.

I was worried about that. Am I supposed to duplicate the definitions in both the challenge (results) and proof files? I feel like they should be in the challenge, but obviously I can't import the challenge in the proof (because the challenge has sorry in it)

Michal Wallace (tangentstorm) said:

I was worried about that. Am I supposed to duplicate the definitions in both the challenge (results) and proof files? I feel like they should be in the challenge, but obviously I can't import the challenge in the proof (because the challenge has sorry in it)

I think the problem with comparator here is more convoluted than that unfortunately. The comparator worked fine here, in the sense of exposing hidden axioms and "hacks".

The issue is that the AI has defined things such as TurynTypeSeq , Canonical , Equivalent and lots more, and the results are in terms of that.

The comparator lets you be sure it didn't use certain trickery to prove what is written, but if all the definitions are made by an AI, all you know is that no hacks were used to prove whatever it is that it concocted. Put another way , "TurynTypeSeq" is simply some string name for "some" definition, and so are the others.

To be certain it actually says the mathematical statement you want, you'd need to look closely and examine the definitions, and consider whether it is a proper representation of the math involved.

You can ask an AI to do that, but you may run into the problem of not being sure which AI is right if they start disagreeing. Overall it seems to be an indispensable human part of the process at the moment.

I get what you're saying, but my question is: once I have the nice hand-crafted artisanal definitions, where do I put them? If they're duplicated in the challenge and the proof, will comparator inspect and determine that they're the same?

Like is it okay to ask for Challenge.thing in the challenge, and then prove Elsewhere.sameThing as long as the definitions of thing and sameThing are exactly the same?
I think this thread / message here is relevant: #AI authored projects > To court the king @ 💬

Thanks for the feedback, everyone. It's much more readable now.

I created Defs.lean which is now the only thing the Challenge file depends on, and I hid the proof of the canonical form because it isn't really important and required way too many definitions. Results is now the solution file, and just mirrors the challenge but with the sorry lines filled in with references to the proofs.
You should drop from the Defs file everything that is not needed in the Challenge (for instance, you only need Canonical1, right?)
